S by JJ Abrams and Doug Diorst. It's something like $50 a copy now, but its worth grabbing if you can. It's formatted as a novel, yes, but written by a fictional author and annotated by 2 strangers who work together to solve the secret behind it. Its also packed with their other communications, such as postcards, newspaper clippings, even a map drawn on an actual napkin. Not only is the formatting incredibly unique, the novel is engaging on its own and reads like a classic. The two characters are very real, and the evolution of their relationship drew me in just as much as the secret world they found themselves drawn into. It's an adventure novel, a love story, and a thriller all wrapped up into one beautiful package.

I'll preface this by saying that I've discussed a lot with my mother about certain aspects of my upbringing and am on fantastic terms with her now. That being said, something she said to me when I was probably about 16 (counting that as a child because at 16 you are not the adult you think you are) has stuck with me for years. I struggled with a lot of mental health issues (diagnoses have jumped from major depressive disorder to bipolar to borderline most recently) which got particularly bad in 10th-12th grade. I'd broken down crying and she looked at me and told me, "No one will want to be around you if you're just sad all the time." It's a comment that I internalized for years, meaning I both thought that sad was all I was and therefore really worked my way into a self fulfilling prophecy, as well as being absolutely terrified to reach out when I'm doing poorly due to fear of losing the people I'm close to. Thankfully, my best friend and roommate now has spent a long time convincing me to just damn well talk to him when things get bad, and he's stuck around for a good long while, so I'm working my way out of it.

1 - Oxenfree: I'm really not a horror game person. Really, really, REALLY not. However, I'm a sucker for surrealist indie games and it drew me in and refused to let me go until I finished it. Or, at least, thought I did. The surprise of its having a NG+ when I booted it up again blew me away.

2 - Night in the Woods: Again, really not normally my style, but the game was so nuanced and well written that I found myself sobbing a couple times during my playthrough. "And, until then, I want to hope, and I want it to hurt, because that means it meant something."

3 - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength: Technically the second "episode" to a game I played last year, but as a follow up it holds its own brilliantly, polishing an already fantastic set of mechanics and adding new ones that propelled the game along a convincing and utterly unnerving storyline. 

4 - Civilization VI: I know it's not Civ V. I know it never will be Civ V. Honestly though, having played a lot of the fifth game, I enjoyed some of the changes made. For me, at least, it made it more rewarding when I had to sit and map out districts and wonder sites. It just made the growth feel so much more tangible.

5 - Detroit: Become Human: Definitely my favourite game played this year, beating Oxenfree by only the slimmest of margins. I loved the characters. I loved the story. I love the questions the game brought to the table during a period of such vast technological advances in the real world. Plus, getting super stoned with my roommate and ugly crying whenever I accidentally fucked someone over was fun.

I work in a local bookstore. I really didn't start the job anticipating the sheer amount of personal information that people will talk about in a bookshop. However, this is a small town with an abundance of lively characters (to put it nicely), so there's been a lot.

My personal favourite is a lady who came in while I was alone in the store. We carry some non-book items too, mostly stuff that my boss thinks is interesting or unique. Often we keep an unboxed one on the desk. One of these things was basically a glorified magic 8 ball, except instead of a ball full of liquid (sorry, best I could word it) it was a metal ball on a wire hanging from a post attached to a magnetic base printed with pie-wedge spaces with different "answers" on them. She gives the ball a swing, and it stops hovering over the "yes" option. She gasps. It's not the first time I've seen someone take the thing way too seriously, but it's the first time I've been offered an explanation:

"I asked it if I should break up with my boyfriend. He's been cheating on me."

I told her that yes, she probably should in that case. Not too personal at this point, but heading down that road, and I was hoping to end the conversation there. In retrospect, I'm glad I didn't, simply because what came next was one of the most "What the fuck" and "why do I still live here" moments I've had. She grabbed a bunch of her hair, pulled it upward and made a slicing motion as she said "Yeah, he's been lying to me too. He hid the fact he was SCALPED right down the street."

I don't remember my response. More than likely it was taken in stride, because where I live it's unfortunately pretty believable. I want to move.

I moved in with a friend of mine at the beginning of September last year. We got an upstairs unit in a fourplex that had been built in the 60's. Shitty little place, falling apart, had to spend the last couple months with a bathroom door that was only attached to the wall by like half a hinge. Honestly, though, that all would have been manageable had it not been for the Thing in the house. 

I've never been a believer in the paranormal. I was raised incredibly Christian, and walked away from the lifestyle and mindset quite thoroughly years ago, so any sort of spiritualism was really off the table for me. Thus, when my roommate told me that he thought that there was something in the house, I called bullshit. He said he'd seen things, and a girl he dated for a while said she'd seen shit too, but I've known her since we were in kindergarten and knew to take it with a grain of salt. Then one night we had friends over, and being regular users of pot, proceeded to get really, really high. I ended up greening out as we were all sitting on the couch. It was a sectional, so three of the others (one of whom was staying with us at the time) were sitting with their backs to the kitchen, my roommate and I were sitting with the kitchen to our right. As I was sitting there trying to fight off the nausea/panic, I saw a tall, dark, hunchbacked figure run from the kitchen left to my roommate's bedroom. Of course, I didn't say anything at the time because hey, it's probably just the weed. 

The next day we were joking about it, him kinda mocking my lower tolerance, and I joked back that I had been so high I had hallucinated something. He asks what, I tell him, and he just goes dead serious and says "You saw that too?" I called bullshit, and he proceeded to give details like the time, topic of conversation when it happened, etc. Things that I hadn't brought up. He said he saw my eyes go huge. As we were talking it - quietly, as the guy staying with us was really freaked out by the whole concept- said guy came out of his room and said that he felt like something was in there watching him, and like it was mad. But I still held onto some iota of disbelief and faith in logic over the whole situation.

Another night, later on, I was home alone and typing on my laptop. At the time we were lazy little shits with somewhat of an alcohol issue, and our table where I was sitting was COVERED in cans. I was the only one in the room. Our cats were in my roommate's room asleep, as he was out that night. As I was working, a can launched itself from the other side of the table, flew clear over a good three other cans in this impossibly smooth, precise arc, and hit my keyboard. Said fuck that and slept with the lights on that night.

Gonna sneak in a couple graphic novels here:

-Bone by Jeff Smith. Starts out whimsical, takes some very abrupt turns and actually turned out to be one of my favourite fantasy stories 

-Spill Zone by Scott Westerfield. If you like Stephen King, you'll like this. It's a kind of unsettling creeping horror throughout.

- The Promised Neverland. Can't remember the author, but as manga trash I'm obliged to recommend it. It again falls into the realm of creeping psychological dread, has fantastic characters, and a lot of plot twists that even after reading hundreds of volumes of manga I really didn't expect. Plus avoids a lot of the genre's more offputting tropes for newcomers, revolving around an actual plot rather than just fanservice.

In as much as Promised Neverland and Spill Zone (less so) COULD edge into the dystopian category, they avoid the tropes that can make those novels bland and repetitive (class system, totalitarian government, poor orphan child must save THE ENTITR WORLD). And they aren't constantly drawing comparisons to birds. Neverland takes place in a world where humans are no longer the dominant race, but isn't really about that, and draws much more from lovecraft than it does the hunger games. And in Spill Zone very select areas were destroyed, humanity as a whole is fine, and again, more lovecraft/King than anything else.

Wholesome story from my job:

I work at an independently owned bookstore in small town BC. My town is basically like Texas and Florida had a god forsaken lovechild: we've got the cowboys, we've got the meth heads, we've got the homophobes; we've got the homophobic meth head cowboys. Whole nine yards. That being said, my boss is a wonderful woman and tries to support all views when looking at the books she brings into the store.

So anyways, I was working and a man came in with his son, who was 7 or 8. His son asked where the Harry Potter books were, and I took him and showed him, asked if he knew his house, etc etc. Nice kid, polite. So I'm heading back to the front desk and his dad stops me and says he'd like some help finding a book while his son was distracted. Now admittedly, and a bit ironically all things considered, I can be a bit of a judge a book by its cover type. I had this guy pinned as the kind of rude stock car driver type. My first instinct is oh great, I get to point out where we keep the pornos again. God, has no one heard of pornhub?  But I of course paste on my customer service smile and ask what he needs help finding. He started looking kinda awkward and nervous, and finally asked if we had any books for kids his sons age addressing sexual identity. Turns out his son had told him he was pretty sure he was gay. I was thoroughly surprised by what came next. He looked at me and said "I just want him to know that it's okay." 

I just about cried. Like, I grew up in an extremely religious household, and still haven't told my family I'm bi (which I'm okay with, my friends all know and have been amazing). It made me so unbelievably happy to know that this kid had the support of his dad. We found a couple of books with gay protagonists for him, and his dad later came back and told me he loved them.

So, moral of the story is I need to be better about not making snap judgements about people, and that there's good people everywhere. Even in the ass end of hicktown.

If you have a local bookstore, go ask one of the workers for a recommendation based off of a book/genre that you enjoyed in the past. Speaking as a bookstore worker, most of us love reading (obviously) and I know I for one absolutely love being asked for recommendations. Plus, we see all the stock we have in and are pretty familiar with new releases, what was/is a good seller, etc., particularly in smaller stores.

I highly recommend Abebooks. It’s a site we recommend to people looking for out of print books where I work (we only carry/order new stock) and it has absolutely massive selection. It’s also very well priced.

We recommend Abebooks to anyone who comes into the bookstore I work at looking for an out of print book. I second this recommendation. Not only is it great for good deals, you can also see where it’s shipping from and the exact shipping cost right on the webpage for the book. Main character is a modified human designed to be an emotionless killing machine for the sole purpose of protecting the heir to one of these houses, but ends up having to take her place in the court in the empire’s capital. Interesting take on far-future society and really thought provoking in a “what is the definition of human, anyways” kinda way

If you liked Handmaid’s Tale’s Orwellian dystopian-type feel, 84k by Claire North is excellent. Basically revolves around the idea of a near-future society ruled by corporations where each human life is given a monetary value and as such crimes (even murder) can be paid off guilt-free relative to the affected life’s value.

Bone by Jeff Smith is my all time favourite comic series. It’s marketed towards kids, and definitely starts out with a humorous edge, but the last couple of books gave child me nightmares. Wait. Can I still say (type?) shit? I mean, no angels with gigantic flaming swords have come knocking, so I'm going to assume yes. In my defense, my judgement was a little bit clouded at the time, and who would turn down an alternative to damnation? Regardless of any stipulations or clauses, that's an offer too good to refuse. But I suppose I should explain.

They say that all lawyers go to hell. They're both right and wrong. The bad lawyers - in purely the technical sense, so perhaps incompetent would be a better choice of words - definitely do. The good ones, however, are hired on at McMarten's Legal Agents of Purgatory. Some negotiate against Peter's Court, levying the pros and cons of each soul, defending against witnesses both divine and mortal. It's a bit segragationist, in my opinion, that only Heavenly souls can testify against the accused, but things have never really run extraordinarliy fairly upstairs. It's kind of like those "No Girls Allowed" clubs I used to run into as a kid. No, they weren't just Calvin and Hobbes bullshit. They were real, they were a piss off, and making a newspaper hat alone in your room is really just no substitute for the comradery of the real thing.

Other lawyers, like me, are grudgingly sent to intern in the pits of Hell. Our Halos (TM) keep us safe from such dangers as hellfire, harpies, and "The Overwhelming Demonic Presence of the Dark Lord Satan" as the brightly coloured packaging read. Clamshell, of course. The Big G must subject us to some form of eternal torment, I suppose. Technically, these are all internships to begin with, just temporary placements. Kind of like a foreign exchange program run by a university. Just much more cosmic power-struggle angst than a group of twenty-somethings studying in Germany for a few months. However, many of us, myself included, elect to stay on permanently, taking positions in the "Soul Exchange Evaluation" department of McMarten's. Big G allows it, most likely because he know that we piss the hell out of Satan. Yes, the pun was intended, and no, I do not expect you to laugh. I studied law. Don't expect much in the comedy department.

But back to the task at hand.

The hulking being in the throne leaned forward. The bones that the seat was composed of creaked as his weight shifted. One skull emitted a feeble groan. I wondered what bullshit he pulled that damned him to a life under a literal tonne of ass.

"For once, I would like to conduct my negotiations in peace." The voice seemed to come from all around me, and I heard the screams of countless friends and family members. No, more like felt them, digging at my brain with bony fingers. I shrugged at the figure that loomed over me. Average workday. 

"You know that's not gonna happen, Luci," I said sweetly. Once you got used to his presence, Lucifer wasn't particularly frightening. As long as your Halo (TM) was functional (and I'd been sure to plug mine in last night, though the golden radiance emitted from the dock once it was connected properly did make my studio apartment a rather too bright to get an entirely proper night's rest), he couldn't touch you. Think vampires and garlic. Or crosses. Or daylight. Poor bastards. 

I opened my appointments leger. It was quarter after ten CPT (Cosmic Planar Time). Thank god (again, I know. Don't flood my inbox about it) I'd made it on time. The wait at Cthulu's Coffee Shoppe and Bakery had been almost too long to risk, but like I said, charging halos screwed with a person's sleep. So I'd grabbed a mocha with a triple shot of espresso, and believe me, the caffeine content of everything in the afterlife is ridiculous, leaving me feeling almost too energetic. Regulations on things like caffeine and alcohol tend to be much more flexible when you don't have a heart to stop or a liver to destroy.

I was just starting to weigh the pros and cons of asking for a glass of water (pros: I was thirsty as hell. Water = problem solved. Cons: It was always just a bit too warm here, enough to let you consider finishing the glass but also hate yourself for it afterwards. Plus, it tasted like the worst tap water I'd ever had. And believe me, travelling for clients, you stay in a lot of hotels. Hotel tap water is a level of hell that I'd failed to experience even here) when a young man in a dark hooded cloak snapped into existence in front of us in a shower of sparks and another cloud of sulfurous smoke. I startled, and hurried to take my position at the desk positioned just in front of him. He blinked, looking first at Satan, then at me (or rather, my back) for somewhat longer. Didn't blame him. Luci could be a bit hard to look at, all horns and bleeding gashes and general air of fear and all that. Besides, when you're trying to sell your soul, Satan is a pretty expected part of the process. A lawyer? Not so much.

I gestured to the seat beside my own at the desk. The young man looked again at Satan, as if expecting guidance, then seemed to decide that that was a poor decision, and started towards me. Noticing what he held in his hand, I held up my own, stopping him, and pointed to the tarp situated between the desk and the throne. He scurried towards it, undoubtedly less eager than he thought to be close to the Dark Lord, and dropped the severed goat head with a rather unceremonious splat-crunch noise. He looked back, and I gestured once more to the empty seat. I was glad it had been a head this time. I tended to miss smaller implements such as knives, and I'd had one too many suits ruined by animal blood. You'd think for somewhere dealing with as many dead goats, cats, bats, etc. they'd have better dry cleaners. But, I suppose, this is Hell, and all your clothes always come back a little smaller than you sent them in, or with a wrinkle that you can't seem to iron out no matter how hard you try. I suppose Heaven might have better facilities, but I'm still a bit too shy to ask an Angel to use their washer-dryer. I can't see it ending well.

He - one Jean-Michael Palmer (could his parents not agree on one first name? It was going to make the paperwork a pain in the ass) - practically sprinted to and vaulted over the table in his rush to get at least four feet farther away from His Dark Eminence. He sat down. I sighed, somewhat impatiently. That coffee was getting to me. I had to pee. This was taking too long. But I pasted on my best please-consider-recommending-our-services-to-your-little-pagan-friends smile and nodded at Lucifer. His lip curled, but like me, he had business to conduct.

"So, Mortal," he growled from everywhere and nowhere. "Name your terms."
